look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST · Western horsenettle has much BROADER, often DEEPLY LOBED green-to-gray-green leaves than silverleaf nightshade. It is a prickly or sometimes sparsely armed upright perennial, with large lavender/blue five-pointed flowers and a cluster of yellow anthers. Later it produces exposed smooth round GREEN-STRIPED young berries that turn YELLOW as they ripen—just like silverleaf, so yellow fruit or purple flowers ALONE cannot split them. Instead check the broad lobed leaf outline and measure ripe berry size (often ~2–3 cm on regional material), then compare silver-gray felt on a typical silverleaf nightshade.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Solanaceae/Solanum: alternate leaves, 5-parted rotate or star-shaped corollas, poricidal anthers, and berry fruits; prickles and stellate hairs occur in many species.
best_field_traits: upright perennial herb to about 0.8–1 m, often stout and erect
ALTERNATE simple, ovate broadly outlined leaves with 2–4 irregular lobes per side (sometimes shallower); typically 5–16 x 2.5–10 cm
surface often GREEN to gray-green, stellate hairy but lacks typical dense SILVER FELT of silverleaf nightshade
stems, petioles and leaf veins may carry scattered cream/yellowish straight sharp prickles, sometimes sparse or absent
lavender, bluish purple or occasionally white 5-lobed star/rotate flowers commonly 2–4.6 cm across
five clustered YELLOW anthers, subequal in length; pale style may project beyond them
young green berries can display darker stripes like silverleaf nightshade
exposed round yellow ripe berries, generally larger than silverleaf: botanical revision 1.3–2.5 cm wide; UT Williamson county specimens ~2.5–3 cm
calyx mostly a small spreading/reflexed collar under ripe berry, not a prickly enclosure like buffalobur
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Broader greener leaves and larger overall build than silverleaf nightshade; much less densely prickly than buffalobur.
crew_field_sequence: 1 · WHOLE SHOOT: Find a sturdier greenish plant with broad ovate leaves; don't identify from purple flowers alone.
2 · ONE LEAF: The leaf blade usually has obvious deep sinuses between broad triangular side lobes. Compare a SILVERY, mostly narrow wavy leaf of S. elaeagnifolium.
3 · ONE FLOWER: Find lavender five-lobed corolla, 5 yellow anthers, and projecting pale style; the style is NOT another anther.
4 · ARMATURE: Check stems, petioles and main leaf veins for spaced pale straight prickles. Some shoots are less prickly; missing prickles isn't exclusion.
5 · MATURING FRUIT: Round green striped berries are shared with silverleaf. Check the SAME plant when ripe: usually larger exposed yellow berry, but fruit color alone will not confirm this ID.
6 · CONFIRM LOOK-ALIKES: Silverleaf = dense silvery foliage and usually smaller 8–15 mm fruit; buffalobur = yellow petals and hugely thorny fruiting calyx enclosing the berry.
morphology_keys.habit: Perennial erect herb, often coarse and 0.4–1 m tall. Stems one to a few from base with branching near upper plant; moderately star-hairy. Do not assume a rhizome is proven from an aboveground photograph.
morphology_keys.leaf: Alternate simple leaves. Mature blades are usually broad OVATE, sometimes asymmetric at base, with strongly or weakly sinuate/lobed margins and 2–4 main side lobes per edge. Flora of North America gives blade 6–15 × 3–10 cm; UT Williamson County treatment documents leaves occasionally up to 20 × 13 cm. Surfaces stellate-hairy but not usually uniformly silver-white like silverleaf nightshade.
morphology_keys.prickles: Cream to yellow, straight or slightly curved, often spaced on round stems, petioles and occasionally larger leaf veins, sometimes absent or sparse; lengths up to ~6.5 mm on stems in FNA. These are surface prickles, not branched woody thorns.
morphology_keys.flower: Typically a five-rayed lavender-to-blue-violet or occasionally white fused corolla roughly 2–4.6 cm across. Five bright yellow somewhat grouped anthers are generally SUBEQUAL, 5–9 mm, and open by small pores at distal tips. A pale style extends from their center with greenish stigma. Flowers in extra-axillary branched inflorescences.
morphology_keys.fruit: Immature fruit can be light green with DARK GREEN longitudinal stripes, as in silverleaf nightshade. Later exposed smooth, tough-skinned yellow berries become ~1.3–2.5 cm wide in FNA/revision; the UT Williamson County account includes ~2.5–3 cm specimens. The calyx spreads or bends backwards below the exposed fruit, unlike an enlarged spiny enclosing cup in S. rostratum.
morphology_keys.habitat: Prairie, loamy or rocky grassland, roadsides, woodland edges and disturbed field sites in Central Texas; flowers spring through fall when weather allows. The species is native in Texas but the repo's exact Hays-specific range/native labels remain PROVISIONAL pending separate county-science lane.
morphology_keys.management: Perennial broadleaf that can persist in maintained beds and disturbed soils; scattered sharp prickles require gloves when inspecting. Yellow berries and foliage are poisonous to livestock and are not for food. If removal is warranted by restoration goals, document patch and evaluate regrowth; prioritize accurate ID before vegetation decisions.

field_terms.Sinus: Indentation between leaf lobes; the deep leaf indentations are easier to show than an abstract 'broad leaf' label.
field_terms.Stellate hair: Branched, star-shaped hair (needs hand lens). Having stellate hairs doesn't necessarily make an entire plant silver-gray.
field_terms.Anther: Pollen-bearing yellow organ around the flower center, usually five.
field_terms.Style / stigma: Paler central stalk, often projecting beyond the anthers, with the receptive tip.
field_terms.Calyx: Sepal cup immediately under flower or berry; in western horsenettle it does NOT engulf the ripe berry.
field_terms.Prickle: Sharp outgrowth on stem or leaf vein; may be sparse or even absent.

field_matrix.leaves: Large greenish ovate blade, often deep triangular side lobes
field_matrix.flower: Broad purple or lavender star, 5 subequal clustered yellow anthers
field_matrix.fruit: Immature green striped; ripe smooth exposed YELLOW, commonly ~13–30 mm regionally
field_matrix.field_decision: Find one BROAD lobed leaf in same plant as the flowers/fruits; do NOT decide from ripe berry color.

field_matrix.leaves: Usually narrower, densely ashy SILVER felt, margins wavy or sometimes lobed
field_matrix.flower: Violet or sometimes white star with yellow anthers; corolla similar
field_matrix.fruit: Immature green striped; ripe smooth exposed YELLOW or orange, usually ~8–15 mm
field_matrix.field_decision: Compare dense gray/silver felt and generally smaller fruit against broader, greener western horsenettle.

field_matrix.leaves: Deeply dissected, green and very strongly prickly
field_matrix.flower: Distinctly YELLOW corolla and very UNEQUAL anthers, one conspicuously long curved anther
field_matrix.fruit: Fruit hidden under large violently SPINY enlarging calyx
field_matrix.field_decision: Yellow flower, asymmetrical anther, and enclosing bur are best; unlike both other nightshades.

field_matrix.leaves: Smaller green ovate blades, generally without prickles
field_matrix.flower: Much smaller usually WHITE star flowers
field_matrix.calyx: Typically bent backward away from mature fruit
field_matrix.field_decision: Small unarmed green nightshade, white flowers, black ripe fruit.

not_reliable_alone: Purple flower — also occurs on silverleaf, several other local Solanum and white-flowered variants occur.
Round striped green juvenile fruit — BOTH western horsenettle and silverleaf often have stripes.
Ripe yellow fruit — shared by western horsenettle and silverleaf.
Presence of star-shaped hairs — both have stellate hairs; it is the gross silver FELT versus greener broad lobes that helps.
Prickles — some western horsenettle individuals have few or none.
Precise species identification from leafless yellow fruits without a scale: postpone until leaves or additional diagnostic evidence is present.

visual_comparison.title: Western horsenettle: BIG lobed leaf → PURPLE flower → YELLOW fruit
visual_comparison.subtitle: Each look-alike panel is labeled as a DIFFERENT species. Do not trust a yellow berry or purple flower alone.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BROAD GREEN LOBED leaves + big purple flower + usually LARGE exposed yellow berries. Silverleaf looks SILVER and often has smaller fruit. Buffalobur hides fruit inside a spiny burr.

items.label: 1 — Real flowering shoot: broad lobes beside purple flowers
items.image_role: Whole top of shoot: very broad greenish lobed leaf blades and multiple lavender flowers
items.caption: Look at the lower large GREENISH leaf blades: each has unmistakable broad lobes separated by deep sinuses. Purple star flowers nearby help tie the leaf to the plant. This is an actual central-Texas Solanum dimidiatum observation (near Taylor). The leaf surface appears hairy but NOT solid silver. Don't identify from flowers alone.
items.why_it_matters: Side-by-side leaf outline is the strongest fast split from S. elaeagnifolium.
items.creator: dsorenson
items.photo_status: External Commons exact taxon and individual CC0 1.0 verified 2026-10-20; actual original 2048x1898 pixel content inspected. Arrow tips target visible large leaf and pale purple petal, no invisible microscopics.

items.label: 2 — Individual flower: yellow anthers vs pale style
items.image_role: High-resolution single five-lobed lavender corolla, clustered yellow anthers, small pale style and unopened hairy buds
items.caption: This exact-species flower makes a good anatomy lesson: the FIVE YELLOW ANTHERS sit around a small pale central style and greenish stigma, while the lavender STAR lobes are the corolla. Unopened hairy buds surround the flower. Even this view is NOT enough to separate western horsenettle from silverleaf without a leaf/fruit check.
items.why_it_matters: Correctly separates corolla petal from anther, and keeps style/stigma from getting mislabeled as an additional anther.
items.creator: Rosario

items.label: 3 — Narrow-to-deep leaf lobes on open flowering stem
items.image_role: Deep green, triangular leaf lobes and pale violet flower in a mixed wildflower setting
items.caption: This is another real S. dimidiatum individual from Ellis County, showing deeply cut greenish leaves and smaller flower in more open growth. The round yellow-and-red heads of OTHER plant species in the grass are NOT part of the horsenettle. Use the big broad-lobed leaf as confirmation.
items.why_it_matters: Shows that lobes can be deep and irregular, while unrelated flowers in the background must not be interpreted as the nightshade's fruit.

items.label: 5 — Ripe exposed yellow fruits on leafless stems
items.image_role: Several relatively large smooth yellow ripe berries, on dry leafless branching perennial stems
items.caption: This is the ALREADY INSTALLED CC0 western horsenettle FRUIT photograph by Vince Hale. Mature yellow berries are exposed and not tucked inside a spiny bur. SILVERLEAF has yellow ripe berries too! A leafless fruit photograph cannot prove the species separation by color; measure fruit size and return to leaves.

items.label: 6 — LOOK-ALIKE: SILVERLEAF leaves are narrower and ASHY-SILVER
items.image_role: Different species: narrow silvery felted leaves and more open branching habit
items.caption: THIS IS SILVERLEAF NIGHTSHADE (S. elaeagnifolium), NOT WESTERN HORSENETTLE. Compare its much narrower silvery/ashy leaves against western horsenettle's broad greenish lobed blades. Some overlap exists, so also inspect fruit size where available.
items.why_it_matters: Paired comparative leaf images are the first true field separation step.
items.creator: Alex Abair

items.label: 7 — LOOK-ALIKE: BUFFALOBUR encloses fruit in spiny calyx
items.image_role: Different species: heavily spiny fruiting calyces and deeply lobed green leaves
items.caption: BUFFALOBUR is a DIFFERENT nightshade. Its fruit is concealed inside the enlarged thorny/PRICKLY calyx. Western horsenettle has exposed yellow ripe berries and a smaller calyx collar. Yellow BUFFALOBUR flowers also contrast with purple western horsenettle flowers.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Western horsenettle: compare the lobes first, then flower and berries
steps: CHECK THE BIG LEAF: western horsenettle's broad ovate blade with deep indentations is usually greener than silverleaf's narrow gray/silvery felted blade.
FIND ONE FLOWER: lavender five-lobed corolla, yellow anthers and pale projecting style. Similar to silverleaf: do NOT decide just from the bloom.
LOOK AT THE RIPE BERRY: smooth and exposed, YELLOW. Silverleaf also turns yellow, but usually has a smaller berry; measure it and compare leaf form.
RULE OUT BUFFALOBUR: much pricklier, with yellow flowers and enlarged prickly calyx enclosing the berry.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Arrows point only to visually inspected organ-scale structures. Leaf and fruit comparison photos are not at matching magnification; estimate size using a ruler on the actual plant.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Do not confuse mature berry color with an edible fruit. Prickles may be absent from otherwise recognizable western horsenettle.
